approachQuestion.prompt: A device protocol P is defined as follows: P(0) emits X once. For k>0, P(k) performs P(k-1), emits Y once, then performs P(k-1) again. Send exactly the event sequence P(d) to an append-only sink. Examples: d=0 emits X; d=1 emits XYX; d=2 emits XYXYXYX. Every event occurrence must be sent, even if it repeats an earlier segment.
constraints: 0 ≤ d ≤ 25. Each sink.emit(character) call takes constant time and must represent exactly one event; bulk writes or compressed commands are not supported.
The sink stores its own history outside the algorithm and cannot be read back. Calls may not be omitted or reordered.
Ordinary calls retain their frames until return; there is no tail-call elimination. Do not count sink-owned event history as auxiliary storage.

options.text: Build the full event sequence in a private character array, then emit each stored character once.
options.feedback: This sends the correct events but retains a removable full copy of the sequence before sending.

options.text: Memoize whether P(k) has already run and skip it on later calls with the same k.
options.feedback: For d=1, the second P(0) must emit another X; skipping it produces XY instead of XYX.

options.text: Implement P directly: at zero emit X, otherwise call P(k-1), emit Y, and call P(k-1) a second time.
options.feedback: Both child occurrences are observable protocol actions, so both must execute in order.

options.text: Use explicit frames storing k and which of the first child, Y event, or second child is next; process one frame stage at a time.
options.feedback: The staged frame stack preserves every occurrence and has the same peak depth and total emitted work as recursive execution.

feedback.reason: The two identical-looking child calls emit separate required event sequences and cannot be merged by caching.
details: Call P(d). P(0) emits X and returns. For positive k, execute P(k-1), emit Y, execute P(k-1) again, then return. There is no cache or private event array; the two recursive calls run sequentially.

The two identical-looking child calls emit separate required event sequences and cannot be merged by caching. They execute sequentially, so exponential output work coexists with only d+1 active frames.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze method-1 as described in the revealed method. Let d be the input level. Analyze recursive method-1. Each event emission and local operation costs constant time. Count call frames; exclude the sink and its event history. No tail-call elimination, copying, or hashing is performed. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair among the options.

feedback.reason: Required events grow exponentially while simultaneous call depth grows linearly.
details: The event count satisfies E(0)=1 and E(d)=2E(d-1)+1, giving 2^(d+1)-1 events. Only one child call chain is active at a time, with d+1 frames.
“O(d + 1) time, O(d + 1) auxiliary space”: Depth bounds simultaneous calls, but both child occurrences must run and emit their events.
“O(2^d) time, O(2^d) auxiliary space”: The sink owns the event history; recursive frames from the first child are released before executing the second child.
“O(d + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This omits both the repeated observable emissions and the active recursive call chain.
